options.text: It moves food along the alimentary canal by waves of contraction
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It grinds food into smaller pieces chemically
options.explanation: Peristalsis is transport, not chemical change.

options.text: It absorbs nutrients into the blood
options.explanation: Absorption belongs to the villi.

options.text: It churns food with acid in the stomach
options.explanation: Churning is the stomach's muscular action, not the travelling wave described here.

questions.stem: Which effect does circular muscle contraction have?

options.text: It stiffens the canal wall permanently
options.explanation: The contraction is rhythmic and passing.

options.text: It reduces the diameter of the lumen
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It shortens the section of gut
options.explanation: That is the longitudinal layer's effect.

options.text: It widens the lumen
options.explanation: Contraction narrows it.

questions.stem: What becomes of the bolus once it reaches the stomach?

options.text: It is stored permanently
options.explanation: The stomach empties into the intestine.

options.text: It is expelled back along the canal
options.explanation: Movement is one-way onwards.

options.text: It is churned into chyme, a less solid form, before continuing
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: It is absorbed directly into the blood
options.explanation: Absorption happens later in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Why is mucus produced along the canal?

options.text: To digest starch chemically
options.explanation: Mucus carries no digestive enzyme.

options.text: To acidify the food
options.explanation: Acid comes from the stomach lining.

options.text: To stiffen the canal walls
options.explanation: Mucus makes passage slippery, not stiff.

options.text: To lubricate the food mass and reduce friction as it is pushed along
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: What role does dietary fibre play in peristalsis?

options.text: It provides the roughage the muscles need something to push against
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It lubricates the canal instead of mucus
options.explanation: Mucus handles lubrication.

options.text: It contracts the circular muscles
options.explanation: Muscles do the contracting; fibre is the load.

options.text: It dissolves completely into the chyme
options.explanation: Fibre stays bulky — that is the point.

questions.stem: Name the two muscle layers controlling peristalsis.
questions.modelAnswer: The circular and longitudinal muscles of the canal wall.

questions.stem: State the term for the partially digested mass pushed by peristalsis.
questions.modelAnswer: That mass is the bolus, pushed along until the stomach churns it into chyme.

questions.stem: Explain why peristalsis works even against gravity.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the travelling contraction wave grips the bolus from behind and pushes it forward along the tube, so movement depends on the muscle action rather than on any downhill pull.

questions.stem: A low-fibre diet slows transit through the canal. Explain using the peristalsis mechanism.
questions.modelAnswer: With little fibre there is less roughage for the muscles to push against, so each contraction wave grips a softer mass and moves it more slowly, lengthening the time food takes to travel the canal.
